item.title: Shoulder — Deep Transverse Friction
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Shoulder and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: glenohumeral/scapular pain, elevation, rotation and functional reach.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, side-lying or sitting with the arm supported.
Begin near a comfortable resting position in irritable presentations.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the shoulder and keep the arm close to the joint line when applying manual force.
stabilization: Stabilize the scapula/thorax when the target is glenohumeral; allow scapular motion when that is the intended target.
contact: Use broad contact over proximal humerus, scapula or relevant soft tissue and protect sensitive anterior structures.
Identify a specific symptomatic tendon, ligament or muscle structure rather than rubbing a broad area.
Move transversely across the target tissue while minimizing sliding over the skin.
forceDirection: Use localized transverse loading that remains tolerable and does not provoke escalating pain.
dosage: Use short, symptom-guided bouts; progressive loading remains the main rehabilitation strategy for most tendinopathies.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Shoulder: glenohumeral/scapular pain, elevation, rotation and functional reach.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Respect dislocation history, fracture, postoperative restrictions, acute inflammatory states and neurological symptoms.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Shoulder assessment → correct regional setup → Deep Transverse Friction → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Supraspinatus Tendon — Deep Transverse Friction
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Use as a short-term adjunct in a selected, localized chronic tendon presentation after the symptomatic structure has been clinically identified.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Sitting or supine with the arm positioned so the tendon can be palpated accurately and the shoulder remains relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: Use a fingertip or reinforced-finger contact directly across the confirmed symptomatic tendon region; stabilize the skin so the movement occurs across the tissue rather than rubbing the surface.
subTechniques.direction: Move strictly transverse to the tendon fibers with a small controlled excursion.
subTechniques.dosage: Short tolerable bouts only; stop before significant irritation. Follow with graded rotator-cuff loading.
subTechniques.reassess: Pain with resisted abduction/elevation, local tenderness and functional reaching.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Friction is an adjunct—not the primary treatment for chronic tendinopathy. Progressive loading remains central.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid in acute tear, hot inflammatory presentation, significant bruising or unhealed surgery.

subTechniques.name: Long-Head Biceps Tendon — Deep Transverse Friction
subTechniques.target: Long-head biceps tendon in the bicipital groove
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Selected adjunct for localized anterior-shoulder tendon symptoms when the tendon is clearly implicated.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or sitting with the arm relaxed and the tendon palpated in the groove.
subTechniques.contact: Use a small precise contact over the tendon while avoiding excessive pressure into the anterior shoulder.
subTechniques.direction: Apply short transverse strokes across the tendon, not longitudinal massage along it.
subTechniques.dosage: Brief tolerable bouts followed by active shoulder/biceps loading as appropriate.
subTechniques.reassess: Resisted elbow flexion/supination, anterior-shoulder tenderness and reach.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: If the pain is diffuse or deep intra-articular rather than clearly tendon-localized, do not force a tendon diagnosis.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute tendon tear or unstable shoulder injury.
